messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: hide informational messages
parts:
On Thursday, September 17, 2015 at 4:10:26 PM UTC-4, Daniel Berman wrote:
Informational Message: The current Metropolis proposal is about to be rejected because of the following issue:
validate transformed params: Gmeasured[k0__][13] is -0.000140616, but must be greater than or equal to 0
If this warning occurs sporadically, such as for highly constrained variable types like covariance matrices, then the sampler is fine,
but if this warning occurs often then your model may be either severely ill-conditioned or misspecified.

This means that the expression that generates the elements of Gmeasured is not positive by construction. In the usual case where the amount of posterior mass on the Gmeasured margins to the left of zero is not a constant, then your priors on the things in the parameters block would not integrate to a constant over the declared parameter space. If the amount of truncated mass is, in fact, a constant, then the posterior kernel is valid, but the sampling from that posterior distribution is very inefficient in Stan.

Either way, this is a problem, which is why we are not making it easy to avoid looking at the Informational Messages. But you can call stan() or sampling() with open_progress = TRUE to look at them in a web browser rather than the console.

Ben

messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: hide informational messages
parts:
On Thursday, September 17, 2015 at 5:50:38 PM UTC-4, Daniel Berman wrote:
This problem began when I upgraded rstan recently. It said that I could no longer constrain a variable within the model block. So I moved Gmeasured to the transformed parameters section and set the constraint between 0 and 1 there. Before I upgraded, I did not receive a single one of these messages.

If it is in the model block, it does not (and cannot) check whether the quantity is negative, so you wouldn't get an Informational Message. But if the quantity must be positive and is not, then you have the same substantive problem whether it is defined in the transformed parameters block or the model block. The problem that the Informational Messages are annoying is minor relative to the problem of not drawing from the intended posterior or not doing so with sufficient efficiency.

Ben

Unfortunately, it's not that easy to do because of the nature of the problem. I'm trying to estimate n, 2n by 2n matrices (G_k) and 2, 1 by 2n matrices (F and E) from measurements of the combinations:
p_ijk=F*G_j*G_k*G_i*E for all i,j,k. Therefore, there are a large number of possibilities that could result in negative values p_ijk.

On Thursday, September 17, 2015 at 6:12:02 PM UTC-4, Ben Goodrich wrote:
On Thursday, September 17, 2015 at 6:04:40 PM UTC-4, Daniel Berman wrote:
Is there an easy way to diagnose and debug where the problem lies? I could post my stan file but honestly, it's a pretty long and complicated file.

You just need to look at the definition of Gmeasured in your .stan file and figure out under what conditions could the expression for its elements yield a negative number, given the restrictions on the upport of the parameters that are declared in the parameters block.

Ben

messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: hide informational messages
parts:
On Friday, September 18, 2015 at 9:44:30 AM UTC-4, Daniel Berman wrote:
Unfortunately, it's not that easy to do because of the nature of the problem. I'm trying to estimate n, 2n by 2n matrices (G_k) and 2, 1 by 2n matrices (F and E) from measurements of the combinations:
p_ijk=F*G_j*G_k*G_i*E for all i,j,k. Therefore, there are a large number of possibilities that could result in negative values p_ijk.

Well, Stan is not going to draw from the intended posterior unless you can make the definition of p_ijk positive by construction (or less likely, have a constant amount of negative mass). If any of the things on the right-hand side are positive scalars, then it may be possible define an upper bound on them such that all p_ijk are positive.

Ben
